By the triangle (chain) law,
\(\vec{PR} = \vec{PQ}+\vec{QR} = 2\vec a+2\vec b\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(2\vec a-2\vec b\), which contradicts its own printed answers for (ii) \(\vec{PM}=\vec a+\vec b\) and (iii) \(\vec{QM}=\vec b-\vec a\) — those are only consistent with \(\vec{PR}=2\vec a+2\vec b\).]

Take O as the origin, so the position vectors of A and B are \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\).
A regular hexagon OABCDE is centrally symmetric about its centre, so opposite sides are equal in length, parallel, and oppositely directed:
\(\vec{CD}=-\vec{OA}, \quad \vec{DE}=-\vec{AB}, \quad \vec{EO}=-\vec{BC}\)
Using this property together with \(\vec{AB}=\vec b-\vec a\), the position vectors of the remaining vertices (relative to O) work out to:
\(\vec{OC} = 2\vec b-2\vec a\)
\(\vec{OD} = 2\vec b-3\vec a\)
\(\vec{OE} = \vec b-2\vec a\)
(Check: \(\vec{CD}=\vec{OD}-\vec{OC}=-\vec a=-\vec{OA}\), confirming the opposite-side property.) [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(\vec{OC}=2\vec a+2\vec b\) (a sign typo) while its own \(\vec{OD}\) and \(\vec{OE}\) answers match ours exactly.]

Direction cosines satisfy \(\cos^2\alpha+\cos^2\beta+\cos^2\gamma=1\).
With \(\alpha=45^\circ,\ \beta=60^\circ\):
\(\cos^2 45^\circ+\cos^2 60^\circ+\cos^2\gamma=1\)
\(\dfrac12+\dfrac14+\cos^2\gamma=1\ \Rightarrow\ \cos^2\gamma=\dfrac14\ \Rightarrow\ \cos\gamma=\pm\dfrac12\)
So the third direction angle is \(\gamma=60^\circ\) or \(\gamma=120^\circ\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints only \(\pi/3\ (60^\circ)\), omitting the equally valid \(120^\circ\) branch from \(\cos\gamma=-\tfrac12\).]

From \(5l+m+3n=0\), \(m=-5l-3n\).
Substitute in \(5mn-2nl+6lm=0\):
\(5(-5l-3n)n-2nl+6l(-5l-3n)=0\)
\(-25ln-15n^2-2nl-30l^2-18ln=0\)
\(-30l^2-45ln-15n^2=0\ \Rightarrow\ 2l^2+3ln+n^2=0\ \Rightarrow\ (2l+n)(l+n)=0\)
Case 1: \(n=-2l\Rightarrow m=-5l-3(-2l)=l\), direction ratios \((1,1,-2)\).
Case 2: \(n=-l\Rightarrow m=-5l-3(-l)=-2l\), direction ratios \((1,-2,-1)\).
\(\cos\theta=\dfrac{(1)(1)+(1)(-2)+(-2)(-1)}{\sqrt{1+1+4}\,\sqrt{1+4+1}}=\dfrac{1}{6}\)
Angle \(\theta=\cos^{-1}\!\left(\dfrac16\right)\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book's first triple \(-1,1,2\) matches our \((1,-2,-1)\) (same ratios, opposite overall sign), but its second triple \(1,2,3\) does not satisfy either given equation at all (substituting gives 16≠0) — a genuine book-key typo, not matching either of the two valid solution branches.]

A vector perpendicular to both \(\vec a\) and \(\vec b\) is along \(\vec a\times\vec b\).
\(\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\2&1&-3\\1&-2&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(1-6)-\hat j(2+3)+\hat k(-4-1)=-5\hat i-5\hat j-5\hat k=-5(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)\).
\(|\vec a\times\vec b|=5\sqrt3\), so a unit vector along it is \(\pm\dfrac{1}{\sqrt3}(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)\).
Required vectors of magnitude 5 \(=\pm\dfrac{5}{\sqrt3}(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints only the unit vector \(\pm(\hat i+\hat j+\hat k)/\sqrt3\) (magnitude 1), dropping the required scale to magnitude 5 asked for in the question.]

\(\vec u\cdot\vec v=|\vec u||\vec v|\cos\theta\Rightarrow 12=10\cdot2\cdot\cos\theta\Rightarrow\cos\theta=\dfrac{3}{5}\), so \(\sin\theta=\dfrac45\) (taking \(\theta\) acute since \(\cos\theta>0\)).
\(|\vec u\times\vec v|=|\vec u||\vec v|\sin\theta=20\left(\dfrac45\right)=\mathbf{16}\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints "1.6", a decimal-point typo for 16.]

\(\vec{a}\times\vec{b} = \hat{i}((-2)(0)-0(2)) - \hat{j}((1)(0)-0(1)) + \hat{k}((1)(2)-(-2)(1)) = 4\hat{k}\)
\((\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c} = 4\hat{k}\times(2\hat{i}+\hat{j}-2\hat{k}) = 8(\hat{k}\times\hat{i}) + 4(\hat{k}\times\hat{j}) - 8(\hat{k}\times\hat{k})\)
\(= 8\hat{j} - 4\hat{i} - 0 = \mathbf{-4\hat{i}+8\hat{j}}\)
Comparing with part (i): \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c}) = 6\hat{i}+3\hat{j}-6\hat{k}\) but \((\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c} = -4\hat{i}+8\hat{j}\) — the results are **not** the same.
Justification: cross product is not associative in general. Using \(\vec{a}\times(\vec{b}\times\vec{c})=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}\) and \((\vec{a}\times\vec{b})\times\vec{c}=(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{b}-(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}\), here \(\vec{a}\cdot\vec{c}=0,\ \vec{a}\cdot\vec{b}=-3,\ \vec{b}\cdot\vec{c}=4\), so the two expressions reduce to \(3\vec{c}\) and \(-4\vec{a}\) respectively — unequal since \(3\vec{c}\) is not a scalar multiple of \(\vec a\) here. Equality would require \((\vec{a}\cdot\vec{b})\vec{c}=(\vec{b}\cdot\vec{c})\vec{a}\), which does not hold for these vectors. [Textbook answer-key error: the book prints \(-2\hat i+4\hat j\), exactly half our value; independently re-derived two ways (direct cross product and the BAC-CAB identity), both confirming \(-4\hat i+8\hat j\).]

Take A as the origin, so the position vectors of B, C, D are \(\vec{AB}\), \(\vec{AC}=2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k\), \(\vec{AD}\).
Since ABCD is a parallelogram, \(\vec{AB}=\vec{DC}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AD}\), so \(\vec{AD}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AB}\).
Also \(\vec{BD}=\vec{AD}-\vec{AB}=(\vec{AC}-\vec{AB})-\vec{AB}=\vec{AC}-2\vec{AB}\)
\(\Rightarrow 2\vec{AB}=\vec{AC}-\vec{BD}=(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)-(-6\hat i+7\hat j-2\hat k)=8\hat i-4\hat j+6\hat k\)
\(\Rightarrow \vec{AB}=4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k\)
Then \(\vec{AD}=\vec{AC}-\vec{AB}=(2\hat i+3\hat j+4\hat k)-(4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k)=-2\hat i+5\hat j+\hat k\)
\(\therefore \vec{AB}=4\hat i-2\hat j+3\hat k,\quad \vec{AD}=-2\hat i+5\hat j+\hat k\). [Textbook answer-key error: the book's printed AB/AD values reproduce the given AC correctly but yield BD as the negative of the given BD — internally inconsistent with its own data; our values satisfy both diagonals exactly.]
